Key ideas

Comparing fusion and fission

Definitions

Low-level waste: nuclear waste usually stored on site for short periods of time and then released into the environment
Medium-level waste: nuclear waste requiring a longer storage time and requires shielding but not cooling
High-level waste: nuclear waste that needs to be stored for a very long time in shielded containers and continually cooled to stop overheating
Plasma: a form of matter in which all the atoms are completely ionised – sometimes called the fourth state of matter
Thermonuclear bomb: a two-stage nuclear weapon with an initial fission stage, which then triggers a much larger fusion explosion

4B

New knowledgeHow much mass is converted to energy in fission and fusion?

Comparing fusion and fission

As we have already seen, both fusion and fission are nuclear reactions that produce energy via the mass–energy relationship, E=Δmc2E = \Delta mc^2E=Δmc2.

However, the processes are very different.

Fusion is the process where two light nuclei combine to create a more stable nucleus, thereby releasing vast amounts of energy.

Fission is the splitting of a heavy, unstable nucleus into two lighter, more stable nuclei, again releasing vast amounts of energy.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 234
4B

New knowledgeHow much mass is converted to energy in fission and fusion?

Comparing fusion and fission

In fusion reactions, the amount of matter that is converted to energy is about 0.7%, while in fission reactions, the amount of matter that is converted to energy is about 0.1%.

These numbers apply whether the process takes place in nuclear bombs, in nuclear reactors, in our Sun or in the stars (Figure 4B–4).

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 235
4B

New knowledgeElectricity generation using nuclear energy

Comparing fusion and fission

After World War II, governments and atomic scientists wanted to demonstrate the peaceful uses of atomic energy.

In 1953, US President Eisenhower proposed his Atoms for Peace program, which reoriented significant research effort towards nuclear power plants for electricity generation and set the course for civil nuclear energy development in the United States.

Similar projects were initiated in Russia and the United Kingdom.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 246
4B

New knowledgeSafety hazards of nuclear energy

Comparing fusion and fission

Nuclear fuel can provide large amounts of energy, but this comes at a price.

Every nuclear reactor produces nuclear waste – a form of pollution that neither the human species nor our fragile biosphere has ever had to cope with before.

Some radioactive by-products from nuclear power stations may be hazardous for up to a million years (e.g. plutonium-239).

Critics argue that there are still no generally acceptable long-term storage solutions for these radioactive wastes.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 247
4B

New knowledgeSafety hazards of nuclear energy

Comparing fusion and fission

There are three types of nuclear waste, classified according to their radioactivity: low-level, medium-level and high-level waste.

The vast majority of the waste (90% of the total volume) is composed of only low-level radioactive items, such as tools and work clothing.

It contains only 1% of the total radioactivity.

By contrast, high-level waste – mostly comprising used nuclear fuel rod material – accounts for just 3% of the total volume of waste but contains 95% of the total radioactivity.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 248
4B

New knowledgeSafety hazards of nuclear energy

Comparing fusion and fission

Although such waste does not take up a lot of space, it is highly radioactive.

High-level waste will take about 1200 years to return to the same level of radioactivity as that of the original uranium ore and many millions of years before it is safe to return to the environment.

High-level waste must be stored in shielded containers to prevent radiation escaping into the environment and must be continually cooled to stop overheating.

Another area of concern with nuclear power plants is the possibility of nuclear accidents.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 249
4B

New knowledgeSafety hazards of nuclear energy

Comparing fusion and fission

Many critics of nuclear energy point to the accidents that occurred at Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011, see Figure 4B–5) as examples of the inadequacies of safety procedures in nuclear power stations.

Supporters of nuclear power suggest that it is an effective way of creating electrical energy that avoids the emission of large amounts of CO2_22​ and other atmospheric pollutants associated with the greenhouse effect.

They also argue that it is a readily available source that is not dependent on wind or sunlight and can provide reliable base-load power.

Nuclear fission reactors are also used to produce radioisotopes that have many applications in industry, medicine, agriculture and scientific research (see also OPAL, Section 4C).

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2410
4B

New knowledgeHow chemical elements are formed

Comparing fusion and fission

Physicists believe that hydrogen, helium and lithium were all created as a result of the Big Bang explosion.

They also believe that all of the other elements on Earth were made during the life and death of stars.

Most of the energy of a star comes from light elements combining into heavier elements in nuclear fusion.

The Sun is currently burning, or fusing, hydrogen to helium.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2611
4B

New knowledgeHow chemical elements are formed

Comparing fusion and fission

This is the process that occurs during most of any star's lifetime.

After the hydrogen in the star's core is exhausted, the star can fuse helium to form progressively heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen and so on until iron and nickel are formed.

Up to this point, the fusion process releases energy.

The formation of elements heavier than iron and nickel requires an extra input of energy.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2612
4B

New knowledgeHow chemical elements are formed

Comparing fusion and fission

Supernova explosions result when the cores of massive stars have exhausted their fuel supplies and burned everything into iron and nickel.

Many of the nuclei with masses greater than that of nickel are observed to be formed during these explosions.

More recently it has been discovered that colliding neutron stars are responsible for producing enormous amounts of heavy elements, including gold, silver and xenon.

Together with supernovas, colliding neutron stars produce all the elements of the periodic table and generate all the elements necessary to make rocky planets ready to host living organisms.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2613
4B

New knowledgeHow chemical elements are formed

Comparing fusion and fission

We are all made of these stars.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2614

New knowledgeOur Sun – a local nuclear fusion reactor

Comparing fusion and fission

Nuclear fusion is the process that powers the Sun.

In the series of nuclear reactions shown below, various isotopes of hydrogen are finally fused into helium-4 with the release of a tremendous amount of energy. $11H+11H→12H+10e{}^{1}_{1}\text{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow {}^{2}_{1}\text{H} + {}^{0}_{1}\text{e}11​H+11​H→12​H+10​e 12H+11H→23He+γ{}^{2}_{1}\text{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow {}^{3}_{2}\text{He} + \gamma12​H+11​H→23​He+γ 23He+23He→24He+11H+11H{}^{3}_{2}\text{He} + {}^{3}_{2}\text{He} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + {}^{1}_{1}\text{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\text{H}23​He+23​He→24​He+11​H+11​H$ Inside the core of the Sun, these fusion reactions take place at very high temperatures and enormous pressures.

The Sun's core is made of a very hot (15 million kelvin), dense plasma at a very high pressure.

It is the combination of the very high temperature and extremely high pressure that allows the two hydrogen nuclei (protons) to overcome the extremely strong electrostatic repulsion as they undergo the various processes of nuclear fusion to eventually become helium-4.

Sun fusion equations (p.173) Series of nuclear reactions in which isotopes of hydrogen are fused into helium-4 (equations in the text, no figure number).

4B

New knowledgeNuclear fusion weapons: the hydrogen bomb

Comparing fusion and fission

The extreme conditions necessary for the fusion of hydrogen (very high temperatures and pressures) in a hydrogen bomb are created by the explosion of a small fission bomb, which initiates the fusion fuel, creating a super-hot plasma.

This means a fusion (or hydrogen) bomb is actually a two-stage nuclear weapon – an initial fission stage, which then triggers a much larger fusion explosion (Figure 4B–7).

Lithium-6 deuteride is used as the fusion fuel; it is transformed to tritium early in the fusion process.

Such nuclear weapons are known as thermonuclear bombs, because the initial fission explosion creates the extreme temperature and pressure combination necessary to ensure that the electrostatic repulsion between the positive hydrogen nuclei is overcome and an uncontrolled fusion explosion commences that only stops when the fusion fuel runs out.

Figure 4B–7 Basic design of a hydrogen fusion bomb and the sequence of operation
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2717
4B

New knowledgeNuclear fusion weapons: the hydrogen bomb

Comparing fusion and fission

Theoretically, thermonuclear bombs can be built to any size.

The process could be continued with energy from the secondary fusion stage igniting a third fusion stage and so on.

In contrast to thermonuclear bombs, pure fission nuclear weapons are limited in their yield because only so much fission fuel can be amassed in one place before the danger of it accidentally becoming supercritical becomes too great.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2718
4B

New knowledgeFusion reactors

Comparing fusion and fission

The practicalities associated with controlled nuclear fusion – to create miniature 'suns' on Earth and unlock controlled nuclear fusion with its promises of almost unlimited, clean, carbon-free energy with no long half-life radioactive by-products – are proving extremely difficult.

Designing the 'uncontrollable' hydrogen–helium fusion bomb was relatively straightforward compared to designing a controllable nuclear fusion reaction in the laboratory that can be scaled up to producing 1000 MW nuclear fusion reactors.

The physics of controlled nuclear fusion is deceptively simple.

Although different isotopes of light elements can be paired to achieve fusion, the deuterium–tritium (DT) reaction below has been identified as the most efficient for Earth-based nuclear fusion devices: $12H+13H→24He+01n{}^{2}_{1}\text{H} + {}^{3}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n}12​H+13​H→24​He+01​nDeuterium( Deuterium (Deuterium({}^{2}_{1}\text{H}$) can be distilled from all forms of water.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2819
4B

New knowledgeFusion reactors

Comparing fusion and fission

It is a widely available, harmless and virtually inexhaustible resource.

In every cubic metre of seawater, for example, there are 33 of deuterium.

Deuterium is routinely produced for many scientific and industrial applications.

Tritium (13H{}^{3}_{1}\text{H}13​H) is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen with a half-life, t12t_{\frac{1}{2}}t21​​, of 12.3 years that occurs only in trace quantities in nature.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2820
4B

New knowledgeFusion reactors

Comparing fusion and fission

It can be produced during the fusion reaction through contact with lithium.

Tritium is 'bred' when neutrons escaping the plasma interact with lithium contained in the blanket wall inside the nuclear fusion device.

Lithium is an easily extractable land-based resource that should provide sufficient stock to operate fusion power plants for more than 1000 years.

Lithium can be extracted from ocean water, where reserves are practically unlimited.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2821
4B

New knowledgeFusion reactors

Comparing fusion and fission

A nuclear fusion reaction is about 12 million times more energetic than a chemical reaction such as the burning of coal, oil or gas.

While a 1000 MW coal-fired power plant requires 2.7 million tonnes of coal per year, a fusion plant of the kind envisioned for the second half of this century will only require 250 kg of fuel per year: half of it deuterium, half of it tritium.

The technological problems of fusing deuterium–tritium on Earth are challenging.

As we do not have the extremely high pressures available in the Sun, the temperatures have to be much higher than the Sun's 15×10615 \times 10^{6}15×106 K.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2822
4B

New knowledgeFusion reactors

Comparing fusion and fission

The deuterium–tritium fusion requires very high temperature.

The temperatures inside the Earth-based fusion reactor must reach at least 150×106150 \times 10^{6}150×106 K – or ten times the temperature at the core of the Sun – in order for the gas in the vacuum chamber to reach the plasma state and for the fusion reaction to occur.

As the plasma is too hot to come into contact with any material it must be contained in an extremely strong toroidal (donut-shaped) magnetic field.

A tokamak is a device that does this.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2823
4B

New knowledgeFusion reactors

Comparing fusion and fission

Figure 4B–8 shows the design for the ITER currently under construction in France.

ITER is designed to produce a ten-fold return on energy – 500 MW of fusion power from 50 MW of input heating power.

The intention is to have a working nuclear fusion reactor by 2035.

It has been estimated that the world has spent over 12trilliononanucleararmsracetoensure′peace′,whileonlyanestimated12 trillion on a nuclear arms race to ensure 'peace', while only an estimated 12trilliononanucleararmsracetoensure′peace′,whileonlyanestimated200 billion has been spent on controlled nuclear fusion research with its potential to generate almost unlimited, clean, carbon-free energy with no harmful long half-life radioactive by-products.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2824
4B

New knowledgeBinding energy curves

Comparing fusion and fission

You can understand the physics of fusion and fission by carefully analysing the binding energy curve (Figure 4B–9).

The binding energy itself is explained in the graph.

The nucleus of an atom is made up of neutrons and protons and there are large electrostatic forces of repulsion between the positive charges of the protons.

It takes an energy, called the binding energy, to hold nucleons together as a nucleus.

Figure 4B–9 The binding energy curve shows that light elements (low number of nucleons) undergoing fusion (joining together) release energy and heavier elements (high number of nucleons) undergoing fission (splitting into two) release energy. The difference in mass, the mass defect and the binding energy are defined and calculated in the rest of this section.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2925
4B

New knowledgeBinding energy curves

Comparing fusion and fission

Iron has a mass number of 56 and is the most stable of all the elements.

We say that iron has a high binding energy per nucleon.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 2926
4B

New knowledgeBinding energy and mass defect in fusion

Comparing fusion and fission

In fusion, the mass of the nucleus that is created is slightly less than the total mass of the original nuclei.

The change in mass or mass defect is due to the binding energy that is released during fusion.

On the binding energy curve (Figure 4B–9), you can see that increasing the number of nucleons in a nucleus up to iron-56 causes the average binding energy per nucleon to increase, releasing energy and forming a more stable nucleus.

Figure 4B–9 The binding energy curve shows that light elements (low number of nucleons) undergoing fusion (joining together) release energy and heavier elements (high number of nucleons) undergoing fission (splitting into two) release energy. The difference in mass, the mass defect and the binding energy are defined and calculated in the rest of this section.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 3027
4B

New knowledgeBinding energy and mass defect in fission

Comparing fusion and fission

In fission, an unstable nucleus splits into smaller more stable nuclei with a smaller total mass.

From the binding energy curve, you can see this difference in mass, the mass defect, between the parent nucleus and the daughter nuclei is due to the binding energy per nucleon increasing as the number of nucleons in each nucleus increases to iron-56.

This increase in binding energy per nucleon is released as energy during fission forming more stable nuclei.

Figure 4B–9 The binding energy curve shows that light elements (low number of nucleons) undergoing fusion (joining together) release energy and heavier elements (high number of nucleons) undergoing fission (splitting into two) release energy. The difference in mass, the mass defect and the binding energy are defined and calculated in the rest of this section.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 3128

We doEnergy of nuclear fusion

Comparing fusion and fission
Fusion
The deuterium–tritium nuclear fusion reaction used in the ITER creates helium-4 in the following reaction:
$12H+13H→24He+01n+energy{}^{2}_{1}\text{H} + {}^{3}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} + \text{energy}12​H+13​H→24​He+01​n+energy$
Note that the energy on the right-hand side of the equation is the kinetic energy of the helium-4 and the neutron – the neutron has no binding energy. The average binding energy (ABE) per nucleon for deuterium, tritium and helium-4 is given in the table below. Copy and complete the table.
| | Deuterium | Tritium | Helium-4 |
| ABE (MeV) | 1.12 | 2.83 | 7.07 |
| TBE (MeV) | | | |
a Calculate the total binding energy (TBE) for each nucleus.
b Calculate the energy released in the deuterium–tritium nuclear fusion reaction that creates helium-4.
Key idea · Energy–mass equivalenceE=Δmc2E = \Delta m c^2E=Δmc2

Working

a Multiply the number of nucleons in each nucleus by the ABE to determine the TBE.
For example, deuterium has two nucleons, so TBE = 2 × 1.12 = 2.24 MeV. Tritium has three nucleons and helium-4 has four. Calculating the values gives:
| | Deuterium | Tritium | Helium-4 |
| ABE (MeV) | 1.12 | 2.83 | 7.07 |
| TBE (MeV) | 2.24 | 8.49 | 28.28 |
b The energy released in the deuterium–tritium nuclear fusion reaction is the difference in binding energy between the final product of helium-4 and the reactants deuterium and tritium. Using the TBE values from part a gives:
E=28.28−(2.24+8.49)E = 28.28 - (2.24 + 8.49)E=28.28−(2.24+8.49)
=17.55= 17.55=17.55 MeV
So, 17.55 MeV of energy is released in each fusion reaction, which is the kinetic energy of the helium-4 and the neutron.
a TBE: deuterium 2.24 MeV, tritium 8.49 MeV, helium-4 28.28 MeV; b 17.55 MeV

$92235U+01n→3793Rb+55141Cs+2 01n{}^{235}_{92}\text{U} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow {}^{93}_{37}\text{Rb} + {}^{141}_{55}\text{Cs} + 2\,{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}92235​U+01​n→3793​Rb+55141​Cs+201​n<br>∣Nuclide/particle∣<br>| Nuclide/particle | <br>∣Nuclide/particle∣{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}∣ | ∣{}^{93}_{37}\text{Rb}∣ | ∣{}^{141}_{55}\text{Cs}∣ | ∣{}^{235}_{92}\text{U}∣<br>∣Mass( |<br>| Mass (∣<br>∣Mass(\times 10^{-27}$ kg) | 1.675 | 154.248 | 233.927 | 390.173 |

Working

The energy released in the reaction is due to an increase in binding energy, which you get from the mass defect and the relationship E=Δmc2E = \Delta mc^2E=Δmc2. Calculate the mass, mmm, for each side of the reaction using the data table.
Total mass before the reaction: 92235U+01n{}^{235}_{92}\text{U} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n}92235​U+01​n
mbefore=(390.173+1.675)(10−27)=391.848×10−27m_{\text{before}} = (390.173 + 1.675)(10^{-27}) = 391.848 \times 10^{-27}mbefore​=(390.173+1.675)(10−27)=391.848×10−27 kg
Total mass after the reaction: 3793Rb+55141Cs+2 01n{}^{93}_{37}\text{Rb} + {}^{141}_{55}\text{Cs} + 2\,{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}3793​Rb+55141​Cs+201​n
mafter=(154.248+233.927+(2×1.675))(10−27)=391.525×10−27m_{\text{after}} = (154.248 + 233.927 + (2 \times 1.675))(10^{-27}) = 391.525 \times 10^{-27}mafter​=(154.248+233.927+(2×1.675))(10−27)=391.525×10−27 kg
The mass defect (difference between the before and after mass) is given by:
mdefect=mafter−mbefore=(391.848−391.525)(×10−27)=0.323×10−27=3.23×10−28m_{\text{defect}} = m_{\text{after}} - m_{\text{before}} = (391.848 - 391.525)(\times 10^{-27}) = 0.323 \times 10^{-27} = 3.23 \times 10^{-28}mdefect​=mafter​−mbefore​=(391.848−391.525)(×10−27)=0.323×10−27=3.23×10−28 kg
Energy released is energy equivalent to the mass defect by E=Δmc2E = \Delta mc^2E=Δmc2. Therefore:
E=mdefect×c2=(3.23×10−28)(3.00×108)2=2.91×10−11E = m_{\text{defect}} \times c^2 = (3.23 \times 10^{-28})(3.00 \times 10^{8})^2 = 2.91 \times 10^{-11}E=mdefect​×c2=(3.23×10−28)(3.00×108)2=2.91×10−11 J
Converting J to eV with the relationship 1.00 J = 6.242×10186.242 \times 10^{18}6.242×1018 eV gives:
E=(2.91×10−11)(6.242×1018)=1.81×108=181E = (2.91 \times 10^{-11})(6.242 \times 10^{18}) = 1.81 \times 10^{8} = 181E=(2.91×10−11)(6.242×1018)=1.81×108=181 MeV

We do4B Skills: Calculating the power output of stellar nuclear fusion

Comparing fusion and fission
A typical exam question involving mass difference and fusion may, for example, require you to calculate the power output of a star. The question will give relevant data including the rate at which the mass-energy conversion is happening (mass difference per second). You will need to know the difference between energy EEE (measured in joules, J) and power PPP (measured in watts, W or J s−1^{-1}−1) which are related by the formula E=PtE = \frac{P}{t}E=tP​.
The Sun converts 600 million tonnes of hydrogen per second into helium with a mass difference of 4.20 million tonnes per second due to nuclear fusion.
Calculate the power output of the Sun. Use c=3.00×108 m s−1c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}c=3.00×108 m s−1.
Key idea · Energy–mass equivalenceE=Δmc2E = \Delta m c^2E=Δmc2

Working

mass difference = (4.20×106)(1000)=4.20×109(4.20 \times 10^{6})(1000) = 4.20 \times 10^{9}(4.20×106)(1000)=4.20×109 kg
Using E=Δmc2E = \Delta mc^2E=Δmc2 gives:
E=(4.20×109)(3.00×108)2=3.78×1026E = (4.20 \times 10^{9})(3.00 \times 10^{8})^2 = 3.78 \times 10^{26}E=(4.20×109)(3.00×108)2=3.78×1026 J
This is the energy output every second from the Sun as the mass difference is given as 4.20 million tonnes per second.
To find the power of the Sun, you need to use the formula power = energytime\frac{\text{energy}}{\text{time}}timeenergy​:
P=Et=3.78×10261.00=3.78×1026P = \frac{E}{t} = \frac{3.78 \times 10^{26}}{1.00} = 3.78 \times 10^{26}P=tE​=1.003.78×1026​=3.78×1026 W
3.78×10263.78 \times 10^{26}3.78×1026 W

Comparing fusion and fission
List three advantages of generating electricity from nuclear power using nuclear fusion reactors. Why are these reactors not yet commercially viable?

Working

Advantages include almost unlimited nuclear fuel available (deuterium, tritium and lithium), carbon-free energy (no CO2_22​ produced), no long half-life radioactive by-products.
These reactors are not commercially viable yet as there is more energy required to run them than is generated by their output.

You tryWorksheet 4B–1 Comparing fusion and fission Q5

Comparing fusion and fission
Show that the binding energy of a deuterium nucleus (12H{}^{2}_{1}\text{H}12​H) is 2.23 MeV.
Use the following data (shown in the table below) for the mass of the particle/nuclide. Use the conversion factor 1.000000 kg = 5.609586×10275.609586 \times 10^{27}5.609586×1027 MeV.
| Particle/nuclide | Mass (kg) |
| Neutron | 1.674929×10−271.674929 \times 10^{-27}1.674929×10−27 |
| Proton | 1.672623×10−271.672623 \times 10^{-27}1.672623×10−27 |
| Deuterium | 3.343583×10−273.343583 \times 10^{-27}3.343583×10−27 |
Key idea · Energy–mass equivalenceE=Δmc2E = \Delta m c^2E=Δmc2

Working

The binding energy of a nucleus is determined by subtracting the mass of the nucleus from the sum of the masses of the constituent particles/nuclides.
In this case the deuterium nucleus (12H{}^{2}_{1}\text{H}12​H) nucleus is made up of one proton and one neutron.
mass of neutron = 1.674929×10−271.674929 \times 10^{-27}1.674929×10−27 kg
mass of proton = 1.672623×10−271.672623 \times 10^{-27}1.672623×10−27 kg
total mass = 3.347552×10−273.347552 \times 10^{-27}3.347552×10−27 kg
mass of deuterium nucleus = 3.343583×10−273.343583 \times 10^{-27}3.343583×10−27 kg
mass difference = .003968×10−27.003968 \times 10^{-27}.003968×10−27 kg
Use the conversion factor 1.000000 kg = 5.609586×10295.609586 \times 10^{29}5.609586×1029 MeV:
binding energy = (.003968×10−27)(5.609586×1029)=2.22588(.003968 \times 10^{-27})(5.609586 \times 10^{29}) = 2.22588(.003968×10−27)(5.609586×1029)=2.22588 MeV = 2.23 MeV

You trySection 4B questions Q7

Comparing fusion and fission
Why are nuclear fusion weapons far more powerful than nuclear fission weapons, for the same mass of explosive material?

Working

Nuclear fusion has a higher mass-to-energy conversion rate (0.7% to 0.1%). Also, the size of fission weapons is limited by the total number of subcritical masses that can be assembled in one place before going supercritical.

You trySection 4B questions Q10

Comparing fusion and fission
How is the binding energy of a nucleus related to the mass difference of its nucleons?

Working

The total mass of a nucleus is less than the total mass of the nucleons that make up the nucleus. This difference is known as the mass defect. It is equivalent to the binding energy of the nucleus, using E=Δmc2E = \Delta mc^2E=Δmc2.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 4, p. 33, 4B-SQ10. Working from the worksheet answers.53

Comparing fusion and fission
Nuclear fusion in the Sun is given by the equation:
$23He+23He→24He+11H+11H{}^{3}_{2}\text{He} + {}^{3}_{2}\text{He} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + {}^{1}_{1}\text{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\text{H}23​He+23​He→24​He+11​H+11​H$
The binding energy for helium-3 is 7.7178 MeV and for helium-4 is 28.2957. Calculate the equivalent energy in MeV, and joules, released by this fusion reaction.

Working

Binding energy of helium-4 nucleus = 28.2957 MeV
Binding energy of two helium-3 nuclei = 2 × 7.7178 = 15.4356 MeV
Difference = 12.8601 MeV
Conversion factor 1.0000 eV = 1.6022×10−191.6022 \times 10^{-19}1.6022×10−19 J
12.8601 MeV = (12.8601×106)(1.6022×10−19)=2.0604×10−12(12.8601 \times 10^{6})(1.6022 \times 10^{-19}) = 2.0604 \times 10^{-12}(12.8601×106)(1.6022×10−19)=2.0604×10−12 J
Energy released by the 23He+23He→24He+11H+11H{}^{3}_{2}\text{He} + {}^{3}_{2}\text{He} \rightarrow {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + {}^{1}_{1}\text{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\text{H}23​He+23​He→24​He+11​H+11​H reaction is 12.8601 MeV, 2.0604×10−122.0604 \times 10^{-12}2.0604×10−12 J.

What were the code names used for the nuclear bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki?
Hiroshima: Little Boy; Nagasaki: Fat Man
Check-in set 1 · Q2b · 4B
Why were two different two fissile isotopes used for constructing the nuclear bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki?
There was only enough uranium-235 to make one bomb. This was used for the bomb dropped on Hiroshima. There was enough plutonium-239 for two bombs. One bomb was used to test that the implosion concept would work (the 'Trinity' test) and the other was used for the bomb dropped on Nagasaki.
